thread.title: GitHub Deal Fits New Microsoft - Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT)

author: The Value Investor
title: GitHub Deal Fits New Microsoft - Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT)
text:
Microsoft ( MSFT ) continues to move ahead and is certainly a more forward-looking company under the leadership of Satya Nadella as it is spending $7.5 billion to acquire GitHub. The deal, even if it is a multi-billion deal, is just a rounding error for Microsoft, yet is what investors can expect and certainly do applaud following the visionary leadership which the company has long lacked.
These advancements have been priced in already, as a modest premium to the market seems justified, yet the current premium is a bit too much to my taste.
Deal Highlights Microsoft is acquiring GitHub, the software development platform with over 28 million developers, in a $7.5 billion deal. The platform allows developers to learn, share, and collaborate on software development, creating quite an interesting deal, in my opinion. Of interest is that the deal will be paid entirely in the form of Microsoft's stock, as the company is not paying cash despite its very strong cash balances.
Mr. Nadella rationalised the deal by pointing out that Microsoft believes heavily in developers, as the contribution from developers in terms of educating the next group of developers is key for continued innovation. He furthermore stressed the importance of open-source software going forwards.
The promise is that GitHub will remain an independent business within Microsoft, as it will become part of the Intelligent Cloud segment in terms of reporting. The deal should be accretive to 2020 adjusted operating earnings, with dilution to earnings per share being less than 1% in both 2019 and 2020. This limited dilution stems largely from the fact that Microsoft will accelerate its remaining $30 billion buyback program, as the issued shares are expected to be repurchased with 6 months' time, offsetting the expected losses reported by the company.
No revenue numbers have been released in connection to the deal, as news reports pegged revenues of GitHub at some $200 million last year, making this a highly strategic deal. After all, the financial impact, certainly in the short to medium term, is very modest.
Either way, investors in Microsoft do not seem to care too much. After all, the deal tag comes in just short of a dollar with 7.7 billion shares outstanding, as shares rose up to a percent in response to the deal. This is despite the fact that the $7.5 billion deal tag is much higher than the latest valuation which reportedly valued GitHub at around $2 billion. Making a deal for a startup makes it crucial that key staff will come and stay aboard as well, which remains a big if. That being said, the deal is too small to move the needle either for the good or for the bad, for Microsoft.
A Look At Current Microsoft For a long time, Microsoft has been a sleeping giant, as it saw some tough years in the 2000s, with shares being stagnant for many years in a row. After peaking at $50 during the dotcom crisis, shares have been range bound at levels around the $30 mark for years, in fact until the year 2013.
A management transition, "reversal" of the Nokia (NYSE: NOK ) deal and savvy purchase of LinkedIn, as well as a successful transition from Microsoft Office to the cloud, created great enthusiasm among investors as they felt that Microsoft had a vision again, and started to deliver on structural and profitable growth.
Momentum has been crazy ever since as shares rose to $50 late in 2015 and continued to rise to levels just above the $100 mark, currently. With 7.8 billion shares outstanding, the market valuation is rapidly approaching the $800 billion mark, putting the company firmly in place in the race to become the first trillion dollar business, alongside Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) and Amazon.com (NASDAQ: AMZN ). It goes without saying that momentum has been backed up by growth (prospects) yet valuation multiples have significantly increased as well as investors grow/grew more comfortable on capital deployment, value creation (instead of destruction) through M&A, and predictable cloud revenue streams.
Becoming More Diversified In April, Microsoft posted its third quarter results as revenues were up by 16% to $26.8 billion. These revenues are split up among three business segments. Personal computing is the largest segment with $9.9 billion in sales, followed by a $9.0 billion productivity & business processes segment and $7.9 billion in sales from intelligent solutions. The company is very strong with exception of the core Windows OEM and Enterprise business, reporting "just" single-digit revenue growth. Real strong growth areas were a near doubling in Azure revenues, 42% growth in Office 365, and impressive 37% growth rate for LinkedIn, among others.
Besides the impressive top-line sales growth, margins keep expanding as well. Even based on GAAP accounting, operating margins still came in at 30.9% of sales, a near 2 point improvement from the year before. Revenue growth, margin expansion, and a reduction in the tax rate to just 14% allowed for 35% growth in actual earnings, as a rather flattish share count resulted in a 36% increase in earnings per share. Adjusting for the impact of tax reform in the first two quarters of this fiscal year, and accounting for a stronger fourth quarter, realistic earnings certainly do top $4.00 per share per annum.
The traditionally very strong cash balance remains with cash and equivalents standing at $132 billion, offset by $77 billion in debt, for a $55 billion net debt load, equivalent to little over $6 per share. If we subtract this net cash position from the current share price of $101, operating assets are valued at 23-24 times GAAP earnings. This marks a decent premium to the market, for an unleveraged business which is still growing at a decent clip, certainly for the company its size.
Final Thoughts I have held shares of Microsoft in the $30s a few years ago and have traded in and out of the stock, but sold out completely around the $50 mark. In doing so, I could not envision the run higher to $100 per share, even as the strategy of Mr. Nadella was laid out and started to sort its first effects at the time.
Reality is that, while earnings have certainly improved, earnings per share have jumped "just" 50% from 2013 levels (aided in a big way thanks to tax reform) while shares have essentially tripled. This indicates that valuation multiple expansion has been the primary reason for the share price appreciation, and not necessarily growing profits (per share).
With operating assets trading at 23-24 times earnings, it seems pretty safe to say that expectations are quite high, in part because investors believe the story of sticky cloud revenue numbers from its still core operating system, as moves into other markets such as gaming, LinkedIn, and now perhaps coding/software development appears to be applauded by investors as well, after the company "traditionally" was very bad in deal-making. Nonetheless, I believe that the current risk-reward is no longer compelling at all as good news is aggressively priced in, and I fail to see triggers on top of a continuation of the growth story.
